pages.text: Pull up a chair and watch that flat line. Without a Network Protocol, two machines staring across a wire only see raw voltage pulses—no idea where a message starts, who owns it, or whether noise flipped a bit. Protocols solve this by stamping strict frame boundaries, sequence rules, and error checks onto every signal. To understand why the modern Internet breaks data into tiny pieces, rewind to the system that broke under pressure.

Spin the dial back to 1960. The Analog Telephone Network carries voices by locking an unbroken electrical path from caller to listener until someone hangs up. Human speech fills that path steadily, so keeping it dedicated works. Computers behave differently: they fire off a millisecond burst of data, then sit silent for seconds while you read or type—leaving over ninety percent of that expensive copper trunk completely idle.

Dialing triggers electromechanical relays across every intermediate exchange to latch shut, and Circuit Switching reserves that entire copper chain exclusively for one session. Even during long silent gaps, Computer C gets a busy signal and cannot borrow the unused wire. Worse, every switch along the path is a single point of failure: knock out Exchange 2 in the middle and the whole reserved connection drops dead instantly.

Between 1960 and 1964, Paul Baran solved both bottlenecks with a Distributed Mesh where switches link to multiple neighbors. Instead of reserving a line, the sender chops data into 1,024-bit Message Blocks, stamping each block's destination address and sequence number onto its header. Using Hot-Potato Routing, each switch checks a tiny local hop table and immediately hands the block to its best surviving neighbor—so when a hub dies, blocks detour automatically without a central map.

In 1961, Leonard Kleinrock proved with Queueing Theory that sharing one fast trunk beats splitting lines into slow dedicated slices. When Terminal A and Terminal B burst simultaneously, a short FIFO memory buffer holds the extra chunks in line, then drains them into the quiet gaps right behind—achieving statistical multiplexing without collisions. In 1966, Donald Davies standardized each self-addressed chunk as a Packet, pairing a routing header with a clean payload slice.

In 1969, ARPANET solved mainframe incompatibility by placing a dedicated Interface Message Processor—an IMP minicomputer—in front of every host to slice, header, and forward packets automatically. The October 29 login crashed SRI's host buffer after typing L and O, yet by December four sites—UCLA, SRI, UCSB, and Utah—were routing packets across the map. That success raised the next physical problem: when two hosts share one wire and transmit at the exact same instant, their signals collide.
